latestUpdates.detail: The player was redesigned on a canvas, three ways, and the immersive one was chosen for both places a video plays: the picture is everything, and the title and controls float on dark fades that disappear two and a half seconds after the mouse stops. The stage now takes the video's own shape, so a tall clip is no longer hung between two black bars. The controls are the app's own rather than the browser's, for one reason: every video now keeps two marks, and they have to be drawn ON the timeline, which the browser's bar cannot do. One is a bookmark -- one only, placed with a key, moved by placing it again. The other is the furthest point actually reached, and the rule between them was his: it only ever climbs while watching, EXCEPT that placing the bookmark resets it to the bookmark, backwards if need be. That reset looks like a bug and is the entire point, so it lives in one place on the server side and the player only draws what it is told. Only what is PLAYED counts as reached; dragging the bar to the end is not having watched it. A video opens at the furthest point, except one watched to the end, which starts again rather than opening on a final frame. Marks survive a video being marked seen. Gallery tiles now show a thin bar for how far into each one he got, and it appears the moment the player closes -- it did not at first, which only driving the real app on a real video showed. Ten sabotages, all caught; one of them was first written as a change that changed nothing, and would have passed for the wrong reason.

latestUpdates.item: A Recommendation tab that judges six hundred saved videos, on a press
latestUpdates.detail: Six hundred saved videos and no way to tell which were saved on purpose. There is now a fifth tab beside the others, and a button on it: press it and the model reads every title, says worth-it, maybe or skip, and gives a reason of at most eight words. The list is then ordered by those answers, best first, and the top one gets a tile twice the size with its reason printed under it. Three decisions are worth recording. THE ORDER IS NOT THE MODEL'S. Six hundred titles do not fit in one answer, so the judging runs in batches of sixty, and a batch cannot compare its titles with another batch's -- a model asked to rank across them would invent the numbers. So each video gets a verdict, which is a judgement about one thing on its own and survives batching, and the order falls out of the verdicts with the newest first inside each band. That is an order the app can explain and the model cannot get wrong. NOTHING RUNS BY ITSELF. Only the button. Videos that arrive after a pass are not judged at all; they wait in their own band below everything, and the page says so rather than guessing on their behalf. WHAT LEAVES THE MACHINE is titles and channel names, nothing else -- no history, no addresses, no thumbnails -- and a test fails if anything else is ever added to that payload. A failed batch costs only its own sixty: the rest keep their judgements and those videos simply stay unjudged. The work runs on the cheap model, which is the right tool for six hundred one-line judgements. Seven sabotages, all caught -- but the one about keeping the order inside a band took three attempts to make FAIL: three items is too few, because a short list is sorted by insertion and that is stable by accident, and forty identical items is no better, because a sort with nothing to compare moves nothing. Only interleaving the bands forced the sort to do real work and exposed it.

latestUpdates.item: A fix that measured right and looked wrong, and a page that never styled its own controls
latestUpdates.detail: The previous entry claimed the collapsed gallery was fixed. It was not, and the reason is worth more than the fix: the check measured a TILE and the fault was in the ROW. Tiles came out their full height inside rows fourteen pixels tall, so each one spilled over the next and the page was a stack of overlapping cards -- while every tile, measured alone, was exactly the right size. Counting overlapping pairs instead of heights showed ninety-five of them in the first forty tiles. Sizing the rows from their contents fixes it, and the check now asks the question that can fail: do any two tiles in one column intersect. Zero, in all four filters, over six hundred items. Separately, the search box and the two buttons beside it had been rendering as plain browser defaults -- a white box and two grey slabs on a black page -- because this screen used the shared field and button recipes without defining them, and in this codebase every screen carries its own copy inside a scoped block that cannot reach another. Reported three times before anyone looked at what the computed colour actually was; it said pure white, which no stylesheet in the project contains, and that single number named the cause. The lesson recorded both times is the same one: measure the thing that is wrong, not the thing nearby that is easy to measure. Three sabotages caught -- and a fourth that escaped because the sabotage itself was wrong, deleting a different rule with a similar name, which is its own warning about trusting a tool that reports success.

latestUpdates.item: The video gallery collapsed into bare lines when it was full
latestUpdates.detail: Fifteen videos drew perfectly. Six hundred drew as a page of horizontal hairlines, every tile two pixels tall. The size of the list was the whole difference, which made it look like a limit and was really a loop. A tile stretched to the height of the row it sat in, and the row sized itself from the tile -- circular, and the only thing breaking the circle was the PICTURE giving the tile a real height. Images below the fold are loaded lazily, so they had no height yet, so the row came out as nothing, so every tile shrank to a line -- and once every tile is a line, the whole list is on screen and nothing is below the fold any more, yet nothing has a size to load into. With fifteen items all the pictures were visible from the start and the loop never ran. The ratio that is supposed to hold a tile open before its picture arrives was being squashed by the same stretch. Two lines fix it: tiles size from their own content rather than from the row, and the box holding the ratio is not allowed to shrink. Found by measuring the running window rather than reading the stylesheet -- the numbers said the tile was two pixels and the thumbnail one, which pointed straight at the squashed ratio; then five candidate fixes were applied to the live page and measured before one was written down. Verified afterwards on the real list in all four filters: no collapsed tiles out of six hundred and twelve. Layout cannot be covered by the test suite here, so the test reads the stylesheet and asks whether both rules are still written; it is weaker than it looks and says so.

latestUpdates.item: The saved-video gallery cropped every clip to the wrong shape
latestUpdates.detail: Short saved clips are filmed tall -- nine by sixteen -- and the gallery drew every one of them in a wide landscape box, which threw away half of each picture before he could recognise it. Videos from the other source are genuinely wide, so there is no single right box. The grid now follows the MEDIA: filter to the saved folder, where every item is tall, and the grid turns vertical and narrow, the tile becomes all picture and the title moves onto a dark band across the bottom of it. On a mixed list it stays wide, because a tall box would letterbox the wide videos into stamps to flatter the tall ones. That rule is about the data rather than a preference, so it lives in a tested function instead of the page. The tile itself was restyled to the app's own guide, which it had drifted from: a panel rather than a bare thumbnail, a perforated film edge carrying the colour that says where the video came from, and a stencilled position number -- useful when the pile is three hundred deep. The badge that said where a clip came from had been drawn in a colour belonging to a different feature entirely, the one thing on the page outside the palette; it is back inside it. Worth recording: the test written to keep that colour out was worthless and said so only under sabotage -- it asked the rendered markup, and a scoped stylesheet never appears there, so it passed with the wrong colour put back. It reads the file now. Six sabotages, all caught after that fix.

latestUpdates.item: Download failed with “An object could not be cloned”
latestUpdates.detail: Pressing download did nothing but print that sentence -- no object named, no reason given, and the video playing in front of him the whole time. The answer describing the video was held in a reactive reference, which wraps what it holds in a proxy so the interface can watch it for changes. Everything on screen works through that proxy quite happily. But sending anything to the part of the app that writes files copies it with the structured clone algorithm, and that algorithm cannot copy a proxy; it refuses with exactly that sentence and nothing more. The payload is now built field by field instead of the answer being handed over whole, which fixes the copy and is better anyway: three values cross the boundary rather than everything the resolver happened to return, since a caption and a thumbnail have no business travelling to save a file. A function rather than a copy at the call site, because the rule is 'only plain, only these' -- a shallow copy still carries a nested proxy, and still carries a function, which cannot be copied either. The tests use the real reference type and the real clone algorithm, so one of them reproduces the failure rather than describing it; if that one ever stops failing, the others have stopped proving anything. Three sabotages, including the shallow copy, all caught.

latestUpdates.item: A video can be opened in its own window, and saved to disk
latestUpdates.detail: Right-clicking a video in the gallery now offers a window of its own, so something can play while the rest of the app is used -- talking to the assistant, mostly, which is what it was asked for. An ORDINARY window: movable, resizable, in the task bar, managed by the system like any other, and as many at once as wanted. Each is its own renderer, so what it should play travels in its address, which makes a caption with a hash, an ampersand or Hebrew in it a real risk rather than a theoretical one; a packaged build also carries that query after the hash rather than before it, which is a difference that only shows up once built. Both are tested. Saving is two jobs behind one button. Most saved posts are a single file and saving one is a download. Everything from the video site, and the posts whose file is withheld, arrive as picture and sound in SEPARATE streams -- so saving just the picture writes a silent film that says nothing about being silent. They are joined with ffmpeg, copied rather than re-encoded, taking about a second and losing nothing. Using the one already on the machine rather than adding seventy megabytes to the app was a deliberate trade, and its cost is that it can be absent -- so that is said in words, with the command to install it, instead of quietly saving the silent version. Worth recording: the first real save HUNG with an empty folder and no error, because a manifest is XML and every ampersand in its URLs is written as an entity. The player unescapes them; the downloader did not. That is the third time that same trap has been walked into in this project, so it is now a named function with a test rather than a resolution to be careful.

latestUpdates.item: A video reaching its last frame was treated as a decision
latestUpdates.detail: When a saved video finished, two things fired at once: the player shut itself and the video left the gallery, marked as seen. Neither was asked for. A six-second clip reaches its end long before anyone has decided anything about it, so the file running out is not the same as being done with it -- it may be worth watching again, or sitting on the last frame. Only the two deliberate actions settle a video now, and both are one click and undoable. The event the player sent for this is gone as well as its listener: an event nobody listens to is a trap for whoever wires something to it next. Worth recording because the first test written for this was worthless and said nothing about it: the stand-in for the player held a video element but did not pass the end on, and a browser does not bubble that event, so putting the old behaviour back left all three tests green. A second one was weak for a different reason -- the page removes a tile before the write and puts it back when the write fails, so counting tiles came out right either way. It asks whether the write was MADE now. Both faults were found by breaking the code on purpose and watching the tests not notice.

latestUpdates.item: About one saved video in five refused to play, and now plays
latestUpdates.detail: The gallery gets a saved video by reading the file link out of the sharing page a site publishes for embedding. For most posts that link is there. For some it is not: the site decides, per post, to send a 'watch this in our app' card instead and leaves the file out. Measured over twenty saved posts, four were refused this way, and the card and the missing link agreed nineteen times out of nineteen -- so the reason is now read from the page rather than guessed. Two routes to the file were rejected before the one that was built. Sending a different browser identity until the site answers differently is an attempt to trick a check, it breaks whenever they change it, and it does not belong in an app he relies on. Signing in as himself was rejected by him, and rightly: it risks the account for a convenience. What works instead needs neither. The post's own page plays for any visitor, and it carries the standard streaming description that says how -- picture and sound as separate streams, five sizes. So a hidden window with an in-memory cookie jar, signed out and discarded after each use, loads that page and reads the description out of it, and the existing player plays it the same way it already plays the other video site. Measured end to end: all four refused posts now play at full size with sound. The window is opened ONLY for a post that refused -- the rest answer in a tenth of the time, and making every video slower to rescue a few would be a poor trade. When even that fails the player says so in words that do not blame the app, and does not offer a retry button for a decision no retry can change.

latestUpdates.item: The most-important-task section existed on the phone but not on the desktop
latestUpdates.detail: A task can be starred as the one thing the day is really about. The phone has drawn those in their own section, under what is in progress, for a long time; the desktop only put a star on the row and left it buried among everything else that was open. The desktop list now has the same section in the same place, so the two screens describe the same day. Deciding which section a task belongs to moved out of the page and into a tested rule, because the flags overlap: a starred task that also has a deadline, repeats weekly and is already in progress is an ordinary Tuesday, not a strange case, and a chain of conditions written inside a template is how one task ends up drawn twice and ticked twice. The order of the checks is the rule and it is written once. Two of those orderings are judgement calls rather than mechanics: something already started outranks something merely starred, because a star is a plan and a started task is a fact; and a finished star goes to the done pile like anything else, since a section meant to say what is left should not fill up with what is over. Eleven tests, five sabotages, all caught.

latestUpdates.item: Classifying an app did not change the hours already recorded under it
latestUpdates.detail: A tracked stretch of time has a category, and that category was decided when the stretch was RECORDED and written onto the row. Nothing read it again, so a rule written in the evening only affected what happened next. On the desktop that is invisible: an app still open starts a new stretch within the minute and picks the rule up, so the row appears to change. A phone app used two hours ago never gets another stretch, so it kept the category it was born with for good -- which is why this was reported as the setting not saving at all, when the rule had in fact been stored and was simply never consulted again. Judging a day is something done at the end of it, so rule-decided rows are now resolved against the rules as they stand on the way out, in both the daily summary and the event list -- they share a screen and must not disagree about the same row. Three kinds of row are deliberately left alone: one a model judged individually on what it was, because flattening it back under a blanket rule throws away the judgement that cost the call; time away from the machine, which no rule about an app makes productive; and any row no rule has an opinion about, since an empty answer means no match and treating it as a verdict would blank every unmatched row. The resolvers are passed in rather than read inside, so the read path uses exactly the ones the recorder used.

latestUpdates.item: A phone block guarded by two rules only ever carried one of them
latestUpdates.detail: The reconciler that pushes standing rules to the phone kept one row per APP, so a second rule naming the same app overwrote the first. The phone was told only about whichever rule came last, and satisfying THAT one opened the app while the desktop — which evaluates every rule separately — went on blocking it. The same mistake from the other side left orphans: the map of existing rows was keyed by app too, so a second row for one app never matched and was never deleted. A row is identified by the rule and the app together now, and carries the rule's id; a row written before that field existed matches nothing and is replaced on the next tick, so it heals in one minute. Worth knowing for anyone touching this: the phone side was already correct — it drops satisfied rules and blocks while any unsatisfied rule matches — so no app change was needed. The first sabotage pass caught only one of the three faults, because reverting either half of the key left the row COUNT right while rewriting every row on every tick; the test that catches it asks whether a settled row is still the same row.

latestUpdates.item: Watch: a gallery of things worth watching, inside Brain
latestUpdates.detail: Brain has two halves now. The feed hands you one card and argues with it; Watch is a wall of boxes you browse. Three sources, none of them anyone else's idea of what you should see: channels the owner marked productive on a large video site, read over that site's public RSS feeds so there is no API key, no account and no quota; his own save-for-later queue there, which the browser extension already read for the recommender; and his saved collections on a photo-sharing app, which the extension now reads the same way because that app publishes no API for saved posts at all - not even for your own account. A watched item leaves the gallery, and the mark is kept per item rather than per source, because the same thing arrives from two sources and seeing it once should settle both. A channel is added by link, handle or id; only the handle costs a request, and a paste pointing somewhere else is refused BEFORE any request goes out, because a typo must not become a request to a third party.

latestUpdates.item: Videos play inside the app rather than in a browser
latestUpdates.detail: The sanctioned embed was measured against the owner's own queue rather than assumed, and refused one in eight: some wanted a sign-in, some had embedding switched off by the uploader. So the app resolves the stream itself through the site's private client API, the way the open-source desktop players do. That is outside the site's terms and it WILL break when they change something; the owner chose it knowing that, and the design answer is that every failure is loud - a reason in plain words and a button to the browser, never a black rectangle. Four things had to be exact, all found by measuring rather than reading: the mobile client chosen at SESSION creation, since choosing per call does nothing and every other client now returns formats carrying no URLs at all, so the ordinary path is not fragile but already dead; the basic-info call rather than the full one, whose extra panel the parser cannot read; dynamic import rather than require, because the desktop shell's Node refuses ES modules from require and the app started with no window at all; and the new file named in the packager's file list, which enumerates root files one by one. The media fetch needed narrow CORS rules on those hosts only, since that session also carries the owner's own data.

latestUpdates.item: A refusal now says WHICH refusal it is
latestUpdates.detail: Every saved-post refusal arrives identically - an embed page with the post data missing - and reporting them all as "the site changed its embed page" blamed the code for posts that are simply private. The site's own documented oEmbed endpoint tells them apart and is asked only on the failure path, so the cost falls on posts that were not going to play anyway: private, deleted, gated, or the one case that really does mean the page moved. A gated post answers with a sentence already written for a person, and that sentence is QUOTED rather than replaced, because this code cannot know who an account lets look or from where. Two faults of the first attempt are worth remembering: the answer was truncated before being parsed, so the explanation was never read; and then it was read from ANY answer including a successful one, which turned a healthy post into a refusal quoting its own caption back at the reader.

latestUpdates.item: The browser extension would not sign, and it was not the credentials
latestUpdates.detail: The signing tool ran, the add-on site answered, and the answer named one error: a manifest description is capped at 250 characters and it was 460. It had been over that for several versions, so nothing recent caused it - the rule was tightened, and the first attempt afterwards is the one that failed. Verified with the linter that site runs, so it needed no credentials and no upload. Two warnings remain and neither blocks signing: a missing data-collection declaration, which is a statement about what the extension collects and therefore belongs to its owner rather than to this assistant; and one innerHTML holding a constant. The other innerHTML was worth fixing and was - it interpolated a value from the owner's own block rules into markup while the two fields beside it used textContent.

latestUpdates.item: The desktop UI has tests
latestUpdates.detail: `npm test` runs vitest against src. There was nothing before: every change to the Vue side was checked by opening the app and looking at it, which is slow, needs the Go backend running, and cannot reach the faults that only appear after the window has been open for a day. The one that prompted this could not be reproduced on purpose, only waited for, and it was reported twice before it was fixed. The pattern is the same one the phone app uses: keep the rule OUT of the component, in a small function that takes its inputs and returns an answer, and test that; a component test needs the Go bridge mocked and every child stubbed, a rule test needs nothing. Where a component test is still the only honest one - whether a control is actually on a view - the page is mounted with the bridge mocked, and that mock THROWS on every write, so a later change that makes a page write while merely loading fails in the suite instead of on the owner's calendar. Every rule was sabotaged to check the test fails without it, which is also how two of the tests were found to be worth nothing as first written.

latestUpdates.item: The desktop Plan can change its day, and no longer opens on yesterday
latestUpdates.detail: The arrows, Today and the date box lived in the Day view's toolbar. The Plan view has no toolbar on purpose - it is a tall screen and a toolbar costs it a row - so it had no date control whatsoever. They are in the page header now, beside the title, shared by all three views and stepping whatever the open view is about: a week on Week, a day on the other two. Separately, the shown date was read from today once at mount and never again, so a window left open overnight opened on the previous day. It follows the day now, but only when you were on today - being dragged off a date you chose yourself at midnight would be worse than the fault being fixed. A related one in the same family: a computed asking whether the day on screen is today called a plain function rather than reading the ticking value, and a computed does not recompute for a function call, so the now-marker kept drawing itself across a day that had ended. The desktop UI has no test runner, so these were checked by driving the real page against the running backend, with the clock faked for the two midnight rules and both of them sabotaged to confirm the checks bite.

latestUpdates.item: This board has a second public copy, on GitHub
latestUpdates.detail: The satellite still serves it at /gangsta/status and /gangsta/status.json, and that is the live one. There is now also a copy in a public repository, GBN18/gangsta-status, for when a stable link is wanted rather than a running server: raw.githubusercontent.com/GBN18/gangsta-status/main/status.json. GitHub visibility is per repository, so one file of a private repo cannot be public on its own - hence a second repo that holds this file and nothing else. scripts/publish_status.py copies it there and refuses rather than publishes if the board stops declaring that it carries no personal data, if it has no docVersion, if it does not parse, or if anything but that one file would be committed. It pushes from the owner's PC with the credential already stored there, so nothing new had to be created or stored for it. Run it whenever this file changes; a copy that is only committed locally is not published, and the script now checks the remote rather than the file on disk to decide.

latestUpdates.item: Presses that did nothing, swept across the whole phone app
latestUpdates.detail: The day planner's two faults turned out not to be the planner's, so both shapes were searched for everywhere. A save that checks a field is not empty and returns runs AFTER its sheet has closed, so the form and everything typed into it is gone with no message: two more of those, a new cart column and a self-written quest, now keep the form up and name the field they want. And a screen that cannot account for itself: the calendar left the cache standing when a load was refused, which is right, but said nothing - so a day with no blocks read exactly like a day that is genuinely clear, and the blocks are the only part of that grid the hub owns. Every other screen already had its own line for this. Three questions are now asked of every screen by test: reading it writes nothing, it asks the hub once, and a refusal is accounted for in words. Two of those tests were worthless until a sabotage pass showed it - all ten tabs share one layout, and a check for what is on screen that does not look at the ancestors' visibility reads every word in the app.

latestUpdates.item: The phone's screens are tested on the PC now
latestUpdates.detail: Driving the real phone was the slow part of every phone change: three adb round trips to read the screen as text, a fresh read after each press because the rows move, and a rebuild and install per fix. The phone app now runs its screens inside ordinary JVM tests, which build the real views, press them by their words and read what came back. Fifteen interactions over the day planner run in about half a minute. Two pieces made it possible: one replaceable seam at the bottom of the hub client, so a test answers for the server instead of the network - without it a screen built off the phone draws nothing but "can't reach the hub", and a test could write to the real calendar - and a fixture day, so no test needs real data. Every fault fixed in the planner was put back one at a time and each one failed its test, which is the only evidence that the suite is worth its runtime. Nothing in the app's own behaviour changed: the seam defaults to the real network and all hundred-odd call sites kept their names and arguments.

latestUpdates.item: The phone's day planner says what it did, where you are looking
latestUpdates.detail: Every confirmation that screen produced was appended to the BOTTOM of its page, below a card that draws a row for each open task, so the answer to a press near the top was rendered off the bottom of the scroll and nothing visible changed. It is a strip over the window now, the same shape as the question that asks how long a task took, and it dismisses itself instead of describing the previous press forever. Eight more presses on that screen did nothing and said nothing: ADD on a task row returned when the band on screen had no free stretch although the button is drawn in every band, and now offers the whole day's openings; four save buttons checked a title was not empty and returned, which the sheet runs AFTER closing, so the form and everything typed into it went with no message; confirming a move with neither dial touched; opening the task behind a placed block, which looked for it in the list a scheduled task has by definition left; tapping an activity row, which has no record to open; and a create that failed without a message. Desktop behaviour is unchanged.

latestUpdates.item: The notes vault is gone from the code
latestUpdates.detail: Searching and opening a notes vault was removed, along with the one-way mirror that fed the search and the invented vault path the always-on process used to satisfy checks that never read it. Four buttons that opened a day's or an entry's file were removed with the refusals behind them, since those records have no file.

latestUpdates.item: Guards that refused without a vault path were removed
latestUpdates.detail: Memory lives in the brain store, and two of its readers returned nothing at all when no vault path was set — so prompts built on a machine without one went out carrying no memory of the user. That was dormant until the always-on process lost its invented path in this same change, which made it live. Four more of the same mistake were fixed: the journal nudge, the journal evidence card, filing a feed answer to memory, and booking a block from a feed card.

latestUpdates.item: Finishing, reopening and deleting a task no longer need a vault path
latestUpdates.detail: All three resolved the task's file name before doing anything and returned the error when there was no vault path to build one from — then wrote only to the store, which never needed the name. On the always-on process, which has no vault path at all, the three most ordinary things you can do to a task answered "vault path empty".

latestUpdates.item: The file relay and the one-time importers are gone
latestUpdates.detail: The relay carried one folder of files between the phone and the desktop; those files have travelled in the store for two weeks, and its read side had already stopped being refilled. The four migrations that moved tasks, daily notes, the journal, the workout library and the shopping list out of the old notes app have all run — their own flags say so — so the code that ran them went too, along with the one-way export that wrote everything back out.

latestUpdates.item: An exercise typed as a hold is logged in seconds again
latestUpdates.detail: The rule that makes a held exercise count seconds instead of reps lived only in the import. That made it true of the three exercises that came across and false of every one made since — typing the hold type on a new exercise left it logging reps. It now applies wherever an exercise is saved, which includes the phone.

latestUpdates.item: The notes app is out of the code
latestUpdates.detail: The folder path setting is gone, and with it the layer that opened a task's file: the task writers took a file name and the file's whole new text, built forty lines of frontmatter between them, and dropped both — the one write mode left has written only the store for a month. The file relay, the four one-time imports and the one-way export went earlier in the same sweep. The tasks folder NAME stays, because it still decides which records count as tasks and which are archived.

latestUpdates.item: Turning a task into a quest works on tasks made since the migration
latestUpdates.detail: Drafting a quest from a task read the task's file and refused when there was none, and adding one stamped the task as a quest inside two nested file checks so it silently did nothing. Measured on the real store: 12 of the 57 live tasks have no file — every one made since the migration, which is all the recent ones. For those twelve the feature did not work at all.

latestUpdates.item: Deleting a task no longer claims it can be recovered
latestUpdates.detail: The phone's confirmation sheet said the task goes to the desktop's Recycle Bin and can be got back. The bin only ever took the task's file, and the writer skipped that in the one write mode left — so nothing went to any bin, and neither app has a restore. A delete makes a tombstone: the record stays, marked gone, which is what stops a device that was offline from re-creating it. The sheet says there is no undo now, and the dead platform code for the bin is gone.

latestUpdates.item: Four switches that controlled nothing are off the Settings page
latestUpdates.detail: Enable and auto-create, for both the day and the journal, plus the filename formats behind them. Every one was saved, read back on the next load, and looked at by no other line in either app — they are from when a day was a file, so 'enable the connection' meant connect to a folder and 'auto-create' meant write today's file. The structs ended up empty and went whole, with the three deprecated fields that existed only to migrate into them.
